result.markdown: --- title: "Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression" subtitle: "Linearity · independence · normality · equal variance · collinearity · Topic 7 · Lab 4" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - We have a model: `sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi + sex + residence + education + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act` - Its p-values and CIs are **only trustworthy if its assumptions are reasonable** - For each assumption today: **what it means → how to check → what a violation looks like in OUR data → what to do** ::: # Topic 7 — Assumptions {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## The checklist | | Assumption | Plain meaning | |---|---|---| | **L** | **Linearity** | The mean outcome changes in a straight line with each predictor | | **I** | **Independence** | One person's error tells you nothing about another's | | **N** | **Normality** of residuals | Residuals are roughly bell-shaped | | **E** | **Equal variance** (homoscedasticity) | Spread of residuals is the same at every fitted value | | **M** | **No severe multicollinearity** | Predictors are not near-copies of each other | ::: {.fragment} Plus a look for **influential points** (a few people driving the result). ::: ## What goes wrong when each fails | Violation | Main consequence | |---|---| | Non-linearity | **Biased** β — the line is the wrong shape | | Non-independence (clusters) | SEs **too small** → CIs too narrow, p too small | | Non-normal residuals | Usually minor if n is large; matters for small n and prediction intervals | | Unequal variance | SEs **wrong** (usually too small/large in places); estimates less efficient | | Multicollinearity | SEs **inflated**, β unstable, even sign flips | ## The one-page panel: `check_model()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_model(m, check = c("linearity", "homogeneity", "qq", "outliers")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s4_assumptions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=1200} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Walk through the four panels. Top-left reference line should be flat and horizontal; it curves. Top-right should be flat; it rises (funnel). Q-Q points should sit on the line; they roughly do. Bottom-right should keep points inside the contour lines. We now take each assumption in turn. ::: # L — Linearity {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Linearity: what and how ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Means:** each continuous predictor has a **straight-line** relationship with the mean outcome. **Check:** plot **residuals vs each continuous predictor** (and vs fitted) with a smooth curve — it should be flat. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.warn} **Violation looks like:** a curved (U, ∩ or banana-shaped) smooth line in the residual plot. ::: ::: ::: ## In our data: age is slightly curved ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} cc |> mutate(res = resid(m)) |> ggplot(aes(age, res)) + geom_point(alpha = .3, colour = col_blue) + geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = col_red, formula = y ~ x) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Residual (mmHg)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s4_assumptions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Residuals are slightly negative in the middle and positive at the ends: SBP rises faster at older ages than a straight line allows. A formal check: `resettest()`. ::: ## A formal nudge: RESET test ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} resettest(m, power = 2, type = "regressor") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` RESET test data: m RESET = 2.7674, df1 = 3, df2 = 535, p-value = 0.04119 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} A small p-value suggests curvature somewhere — **but look at the plot** to see *where* and *how much*. ::: ## What to do about non-linearity ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_quad <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g + age + I(age^2) + bmi + sex + residence + education + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act, data = cc) anova(m, m_quad) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi + sex + residence + education + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act Model 2: sbp ~ salt_g + age + I(age^2) + bmi + sex + residence + education + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 538 98422 2 537 97336 1 1085.6 5.9891 0.01471 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Add a **squared term** (`I(age^2)`) — the improvement is significant - Better still for flexible shapes: **splines** (`splines::ns()`, `mgcv`) — mentioned in Session 6 - Or **categorise** (age bands) — simple but throws information away - Or **transform** the predictor (e.g. log) when the curve is monotonic ::: # I — Independence {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Independence: what and how ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Means:** the residual of one person carries no information about another's. **Typically violated by:** people in the same **village / household / clinic**, **repeated measures** on the same person, **time series**. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Check:** *by design first* (how were people sampled?), then plot residuals **by cluster** and estimate the **intraclass correlation**. ::: ::: ## In our data: people are clustered in 20 villages ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} cc |> mutate(res = resid(m)) |> ggplot(aes(reorder(village, res, FUN = median), res)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "#d6eaf8") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) + labs(x = "Village (ordered by median residual)", y = "Residual (mmHg)") + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = .5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s4_assumptions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ## How big is the clustering? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a <- anova(lm(resid(m) ~ factor(cc$village))) msb <- a$`Mean Sq`[1]; msw <- a$`Mean Sq`[2]; k <- mean(table(cc$village)) icc <- (msb - msw) / (msb + (k - 1) * msw) c(ICC = round(icc, 3), design_effect = round(1 + (k - 1) * icc, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ICC design_effect 0.058 2.530 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **ICC ≈ 0.06**: about 6% of the residual variation lies *between* villages - **Design effect ≈ 2.5**: for village-level exposures the standard errors may be too small by about √2.5 ≈ **1.6×** ::: ## What to do about non-independence ::: {.warn} In this workshop we only **detect and discuss** the village clustering — we do **not** model it. ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Mixed models** with a random intercept per village (`lme4`) - **GEE** (`geepack`) or **cluster-robust standard errors** - **Survey-design methods** for complex samples such as NFHS (`survey`) - At minimum: **report** the design, state the limitation, and be cautious with village-level predictors (e.g., residence) ::: # N — Normality {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Normality of residuals: what and how ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Means:** the **residuals** (not the outcome!) are roughly bell-shaped. **Check:** **Q–Q plot** — points should follow the diagonal; a histogram; tests are secondary. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.key} With n ≈ 550, the **central limit theorem** protects CIs for β. Normality matters most for **small samples** and **prediction intervals**. ::: ::: ::: ## In our data ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} augment(m) |> ggplot(aes(sample = .std.resid)) + stat_qq(alpha = .5, colour = col_blue) + stat_qq_line(colour = col_red, linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Standardised residuals") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s4_assumptions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_normality(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` OK: residuals appear as normally distributed (p = 0.882). ``` ::: ::: ## If normality is badly violated ::: {.incremental} - Check for **outliers** or data errors first - **Transform** the outcome (e.g., `log(sbp)`) — then interpret as % change - **Bootstrap** the CIs (no normality assumption) - **Robust regression** (`MASS::rlm`) or a different model for the outcome type ::: # E — Equal variance {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Homoscedasticity: what and how ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Means:** the spread of residuals is the **same** at every fitted value. **Check:** residuals vs fitted — a **funnel** (fan) shape means variance grows with the mean. **Breusch–Pagan** test. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.warn} Biological outcomes often get **more variable at higher levels**: older adults vary more in BP. ::: ::: ::: ## In our data: SBP varies more in older adults ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} cc |> mutate(res = resid(m), age_band = cut(age, c(29, 39, 49, 59, 69), labels = c("30–39", "40–49", "50–59", "60–69"))) |> ggplot(aes(age_band, res)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "#d6eaf8") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) + labs(x = "Age band", y = "Residual (mmHg)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s4_assumptions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ## Tests for non-constant variance ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_heteroscedasticity(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Warning: Heteroscedasticity (non-constant error variance) detected (p < .001). ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} bptest(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` studentized Breusch-Pagan test data: m BP = 22.89, df = 12, p-value = 0.02867 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Both flag non-constant variance. They are **variants** of the Breusch–Pagan test (the second is the studentised, more robust version), so their p-values differ slightly — **name the test you used**. The effect is **mild**: residual SD roughly **12 mmHg** under 45 vs **15 mmHg** at 55+. ::: ## What to do about unequal variance ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rob <- coeftest(m, vcov. = sandwich::vcovHC(m, type = "HC3")) tibble(term = names(coef(m)), SE_usual = round(summary(m)$coefficients[, 2], 3), SE_robust = round(rob[, 2], 3)) |> filter(term %in% c("salt_g", "age", "bmi", "sexMale")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 term SE_usual SE_robust 1 salt_g 0.302 0.3 2 age 0.062 0.062 3 bmi 0.182 0.173 4 sexMale 1.29 1.30 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Robust (sandwich) SEs**: same β, honest SEs — the easiest fix (`sandwich::vcovHC`) - **Transform** the outcome (e.g., `log(sbp)`) or use **weighted least squares** - Our violation is **mild**: conclusions do not change — but you should know and say so ::: # M — Multicollinearity {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Multicollinearity: what and how ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Means:** two or more predictors carry **nearly the same information**, so the model cannot tell their effects apart. **Check:** correlation matrix and **VIF**. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.key} **VIF** = how much a coefficient's variance is inflated by correlation with the other predictors. Rule of thumb: **> 5** worry, **> 10** serious. ::: ::: ::: ## In our data: BMI and waist ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(cc, aes(bmi, waist)) + geom_point(alpha = .35, colour = col_blue) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = col_red, formula = y ~ x) + annotate("text", x = 16, y = 125, hjust = 0, size = 6, label = paste0("r = ", round(cor(cc$bmi, cc$waist), 2))) + labs(x = "BMI (kg/m²)", y = "Waist (cm)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s4_assumptions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ## VIF with both in the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_both <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi + waist, data = cc) check_collinearity(m_both) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Check for Multicollinearity Low Correlation Term VIF VIF 95% CI adj. VIF Tolerance Tolerance 95% CI salt_g 1.32 [1.21, 1.49] 1.15 0.76 [0.67, 0.82] age 1.14 [1.06, 1.30] 1.07 0.88 [0.77, 0.94] High Correlation Term VIF VIF 95% CI adj. VIF Tolerance Tolerance 95% CI bmi 10.26 [8.79, 12.02] 3.20 0.10 [0.08, 0.11] waist 10.03 [8.59, 11.74] 3.17 0.10 [0.09, 0.12] ``` ::: ::: ## What collinearity does to the estimates ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_bmi <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi, data = cc) bind_rows(`BMI alone` = tidy(m_bmi), `BMI + waist` = tidy(m_both), .id = "model") |> filter(term == "bmi") |> select(model, estimate, std.error, p.value) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 model estimate std.error p.value 1 BMI alone 0.814 0.182 0.00000957 2 BMI + waist -0.537 0.528 0.31 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.bad} With waist added, the **BMI coefficient shrinks toward zero (and can flip sign)** while its **SE roughly triples** — each variable "steals" the other's effect. ::: ::: ## How to handle collinearity ::: {.incremental} - **Choose one** on clinical grounds (BMI for an exposure of interest; waist if central adiposity is the question) — **our fix** - **Combine** into one measure (e.g., a ratio or first principal component) - **Centre** predictors if the collinearity comes from polynomial or interaction terms - **Penalised regression** (ridge/lasso — `glmnet`) when many correlated predictors - Do **not** drop by p-value alone ::: # Influential points {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## A few people can drive a result ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} infl <- augment(m) |> mutate(row = row_number()) |> arrange(desc(.cooksd)) |> select(row, sbp, salt_g, age, .std.resid, .cooksd) |> head(5) infl |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 6 row sbp salt_g age .std.resid .cooksd 1 382 192 8.7 63 3.19 0.025 2 456 173 8 65 2.77 0.021 3 357 104 9 64 -3.02 0.019 4 337 109 12.7 49 -2.76 0.016 5 463 182 8.3 68 2.58 0.015 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} check_outliers(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` OK: No outliers detected. - Based on the following method and threshold: cook (0.84). - For variable: (Whole model) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Cook's distance** flags people whose removal would change the fit most - First **check data entry**; refit **with and without** them; report if conclusions change - Do not delete people just because they are inconvenient ::: ## All five assumptions on one slide {.smaller} | Assumption | Check | In our data | What we do | |---|---|---|---| | Linearity | Residuals vs predictor, RESET | Slight age curvature | Add `age²` / spline | | Independence | Design, residuals by cluster, ICC | Village ICC ≈ 0.06 | Mixed / GEE / robust SE (beyond today) | | Normality | Q–Q plot | Acceptable | None needed (n large) | | Equal variance | Residuals vs fitted, BP test | Variance rises with age (mild) | Robust SE | | Collinearity | VIF | BMI & waist: VIF ≈ 10 | Keep one | ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 4 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `regression-workshop/labs/lab4_assumptions.R` - `check_model()` panel · residuals vs age - normality and heteroscedasticity tests - VIF with **waist + BMI** — then **fix it** - Squared age term · robust SEs · village residuals ::: **Time:** 40 minutes · answer Q1–Q5 in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s4q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="op8h3l.yhxmme" data-show="QWRkIGEgc3F1YXJlZCBhZ2UgdGVybSB0byB0aGUgbW9kZWw=" data-explain="QSBVLXNoYXBlZCByZXNpZHVhbCBwYXR0ZXJuIHNpZ25hbHMgY3VydmF0dXJlIGluIGFnZS4g QSBzcXVhcmVkIHRlcm0gKG9yIGEgc3BsaW5lKSBsZXRzIHRoZSBmaXR0ZWQgbGluZSBiZW5k Lg=="} The smoothed line through the residuals plotted against age is a shallow U-shape. What is the most direct fix? - Add a squared age term to the model - Drop age from the model entirely - Log-transform the salt intake variable - Remove the oldest participants from the data ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s4q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="op8ucd.yhy13u" data-show="S2VlcCBvbmUgb24gY2xpbmljYWwgZ3JvdW5kcywgb3IgY29tYmluZSB0aGVt" data-explain="VklGIGFib3ZlIDEwIHNpZ25hbHMgc2VyaW91cyBjb2xsaW5lYXJpdHkuIENob29zZSBvbmUg bWVhc3VyZSBmcm9tIHRoZSByZXNlYXJjaCBxdWVzdGlvbiAob3IgY29tYmluZSB0aGVtKSwg bm90IGZyb20gcC12YWx1ZXMgYWxvbmUu"} BMI and waist (r = 0.95) both enter a model and each has a VIF of about 10. What is the best response? - Keep both, since a high VIF does no harm - Drop whichever variable has the larger p-value - Log-transform the outcome and refit the model - Keep one on clinical grounds, or combine them ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s4q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="op97l2.yhyfl7" data-show="dGhlIHN0YW5kYXJkIGVycm9ycyB0b28gc21hbGwgZm9yIHZpbGxhZ2UtbGV2ZWwgdHJhaXRz " data-explain="Q2x1c3RlcmVkIG9ic2VydmF0aW9ucyBhcmUgbm90IGluZGVwZW5kZW50LCBzbyB0aGUgZWZm ZWN0aXZlIHNhbXBsZSBzaXplIGlzIGJlbG93IG4gYW5kIG5haXZlIFNFcyBhcmUgdG9vIHNt YWxsLCBlc3BlY2lhbGx5IGZvciB2aWxsYWdlLWxldmVsIHByZWRpY3RvcnMu"} Participants are sampled from 20 villages that share influences on blood pressure. Ignoring this mainly makes… - the regression coefficients biased towards zero overall - the residuals markedly non-normal within each village - the R² smaller than it would otherwise be - the standard errors too small for village-level traits ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s4q4" data-type="fill" data-hashes="30h66g.lr1dt2,piqgu1.mcl5vi,tskrsz.udweix,7o631o.qy7uec,63wamh.uxso16" data-show="ZXF1YWwgdmFyaWFuY2U=" data-explain="QSBmdW5uZWwgbWVhbnMgcmVzaWR1YWwgc3ByZWFkIGNoYW5nZXMgd2l0aCB0aGUgZml0dGVk IHZhbHVlOiBoZXRlcm9zY2VkYXN0aWNpdHkuIFJvYnVzdCAoc2FuZHdpY2gpIFNFcyBhcmUg YW4gZWFzeSByZW1lZHku"} Residuals plotted against fitted values fan out like a funnel. Which assumption is violated? (two words) ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s4q5" data-type="fill" data-hashes="42ki6r.2v42is,a0guhu.o9b9sn" data-show="MTA=" data-explain="VklGID0gMSAvICgxIOKIkiBSwrIpID0gMSAvIDAuMTAgPSAxMCwgd2hpY2ggaXMgYWxyZWFk eSBpbiB0aGUgc2VyaW91cyByYW5nZS4="} When one predictor is regressed on all the others, R² = 0.90. What is its variance inflation factor? (whole number) ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **LINE + M**: linearity, independence, normality, equal variance — plus collinearity - **Plot first**, test second; tests are over-sensitive when n is large - Match the **fix to the violation**: curve → add a term; variance → robust SE; clusters → mixed/GEE; collinearity → keep one - **Report** what you checked and what you did about it ::: **Next:** Session 5 — logistic regression

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
